The corresponding trace formula is analogous to Selberg’s, but more delicate, since it involves both

I will mention various generalizations of the Riemann zeta function, which broaden the perspective

while no analogue of the Riemann Hypothesis is known in these cases, they have nonetheless given

tion: a strategy towards RH which fits entirely within Riemann’s own mathematical outlook, as
exemplified for instance by his proof of the conformal mapping theorem. Importantly, this strategy
requires only the mathematical concepts and tools available in 1859.

The proof of Hadamard that ζ (s) ̸= 0 for ℜ(s) = 1 contains a beautiful idea that can be understood
through the phases of prime powers and reduced to (−1)2 = 1. Indeed if for some real number

expansion of − log(1 − p−it+ϵ ). But then the complex numbers p−2it would tend to accumulate at
1, thus creating a pole of the zeta function at 1 + 2it which is impossible unless 2t = 0.

The Lindelöf Hypothesis states that |ζ (1/2 + it)| ≪ tϵ for any ϵ > 0. If σ is real, then µ (σ ) is
defined to be the infimum of all real numbers α such that |ζ (σ + it)| = O (tα ). One has µ (σ ) = 0
for σ > 1, and the functional equation implies that µ (σ ) = µ (1 − σ ) − σ + 1/2. The Phragmén-
Lindelöf theorem implies that µ is a convex function. The Lindelöf hypothesis states µ (1/2) = 0,
which together with the above properties of µ implies that µ (σ ) is 0 for σ ≥ 1/2 and 1/2 − σ
for σ ≤ 1/2. While weaker than RH, it would still have significant applications to moments of
L-functions and subconvexity problems.

breakthrough by resolving the analogue of the hypothesis for global fields of finite characteristic.

The scattering approach, developed by Faddeev and Pavlov, interprets the zeros of ζ (s) as reso-
nances (poles of the scattering matrix) of a certain quantum mechanical system. The Berry-Keating
conjecture [3] suggests connections to classical chaotic Hamiltonian systems whose quantization
might yield the desired operator. Specific proposals include H = 21 ( xp + px) (where x is posi-
tion and p is momentum) with appropriate boundary conditions, though rigorous constructions
remain elusive. The connection to quantum chaos is reinforced by the statistical properties of the
zeros matching those of quantum chaotic systems.

endowed with the étale topology mirrors the way knots can be interlaced in S3 . This vision opened
a new topological imagination for number theory, suggesting that the geometry of primes might

after.text:
3.4.3   Quantum chaos:
The field of quantum chaos studies the quantum mechanics of classically chaotic systems. The
Berry-Tabor conjecture states that quantum systems with integrable classical limits have Poisson
statistics for their eigenvalues, while those with chaotic classical limits follow random matrix statis-
tics (GUE for time-reversal invariant systems). The appearance of GUE statistics for zeta zeros sug-
gests they arise from quantizing a chaotic classical system [3]. Specific proposals include billiards
in certain domains or more abstract dynamical systems.

3.5     Noncommutative Geometry
3.5.1   Connes’ trace formula
Connes developed a trace formula in the context of noncommutative geometry8 that recovers Weil’s
explicit formula for the zeros of ζ (s) and of L-functions [17, 18]. The key insight is to work with the
noncommutative space of adele classes A/Q∗ , where A is the ring of adeles. On this space, there is
a natural action of the idele class group GL(A)/Q∗ ≃ Ẑ∗ × R∗+ . The trace formula relates:
   • Spectral side: contributions from the zeros of L-functions with Grössencharakter.
